PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact : Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters : California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents : California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
CON
Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR

3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact : Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters : California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents : California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
CON
Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

# Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
## Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
### Additional Titles
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
### Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering.
874,641 valid signatures were required.
The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents.
These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 through 2030.
Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent.
Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets.
The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.

Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030.

Proposition 3 : Make high-income tax rates permanent
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates on high earners that voters first approved in 2012 (Proposition 30) and extended in 2016 (Proposition 55). Those rates are now set to expire in 2031. They apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers (2025 levels, adjusted for inflation).
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 3
Who pays Top 2% of taxpayers: income over about $371,000 single or $742,000 joint (2025)
Revenue kept $5 billion to $15 billion a year starting in 2031 (Legislative Analyst)
Vote needed Simple majority
Money raised, Jan. 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $79.32 million (main committee). Against: $5,500
Largest donor California Teachers Association, $60.50 million (76.3%)
Outside spending Against: $53,500 by Reform California (shared with other props). For: about $155,000
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 58% yes, 41% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 54% yes, 37% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , The details , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 3 mean?
An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
What does a no vote on Proposition 3 mean?
An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
What would Proposition 3 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates the state would keep $5 billion to $15 billion a year in income tax revenue that would otherwise end in 2031. The amount would swing with the stock market. Roughly 40% would go to schools and community colleges, and the rest to other state programs, with part set aside in budget reserves.
What it means for the City of LA
The City of Los Angeles would not receive this money directly. The school share goes to school districts and community colleges, such as LAUSD and the Los Angeles Community College District, which are separate governments; the LAUSD board endorsed Proposition 3 in August 2026. The rest supports the state General Fund, which pays for state programs used in the City, including homelessness grants to local governments. City residents with incomes above the thresholds would keep paying the higher rates after 2031.
The details
Official title Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
This is not the Proposition 3 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the constitutional amendment on the right to marry, which passed with 62.6% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 3 passes
Top income tax rates 10.3%, 11.3% and 12.3% on income above the thresholds, through the 2030 tax year; they expire in 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The same rates, with no end date (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Who pays About the top 2% of taxpayers, who pay about half of all state income taxes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). 2025 thresholds: about $371,000 single, $742,000 joint, $505,000 head of household (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same, with thresholds still adjusted each year for inflation (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Revenue Recently about $10 billion a year, the Budget Center says (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) $5 billion to $15 billion a year kept after 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Where it goes Deposited in the Education Protection Account: 89% to K-12 schools, 11% to community colleges (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same. Because the money counts toward the state’s school funding guarantee, the Analyst says roughly 40% ends up as added school funding and the rest supports other programs and reserves (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Local control and audits School boards decide how to spend it in public meetings, may not use it for administrators’ pay, must post an annual accounting online, and must have it checked in their annual audit (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)) Unchanged (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6))
Medi-Cal formula from Prop 55 A formula that could send some revenue to Medi-Cal; the Budget Center says it has never done so (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The measure lets it expire (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/))
For the City of Los Angeles:
No money goes to the City directly. The school share is paid to school districts, county offices of education, charter schools and community college districts (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). In Los Angeles those are LAUSD and other districts, and the Los Angeles Community College District, which are separate from City government.
LAUSD’s position. The LAUSD Board of Education adopted a resolution in support of Proposition 3, introduced by board members Rivas and Schmerelson, on Aug. 25, 2026 (LAUSD Res-006-26/27 (https://lausd.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8145&GUID=AE05159C-03AD-47C2-B5B1-19227D526555)).
Through the state budget. The Budget Center says the revenue has freed General Fund money for other programs, and lists the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) grants to local governments among the programs created since 2012 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). The City budgets HHAP money (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf)). Neither the Analyst nor the Budget Center estimates the effect on any city.
Who in the City pays. City residents with taxable income above the thresholds would keep paying the higher rates. We did not find official data on how many City residents pay them.
We found no City Council position on Proposition 3 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 3 is a citizen initiative (No. 25-0016). It amends Section 36 of Article XIII of the State Constitution (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Nov. 4, 2025: The Attorney General issued the title and summary. The proponents are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Jan. 13, 2026: Proponents reported reaching 25% of the needed signatures (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
June 10, 2026: Counties’ random samples projected 1,151,120 valid signatures from 1,648,745 submitted, against 874,641 needed, so the measure became eligible. Los Angeles County received 454,802 signatures, 314,836 of them projected valid (SOS random sample count (http://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1993-randomsample-06-10-26.pdf)). The campaign paid Democracy Werks California 2024, LLC $17,435,148.50 for petition and related work (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The tax is a general income tax rate, not a local special tax, so the two-thirds rules for local special taxes and Proposition 43 do not apply to it (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Prop 43 title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 30 (November 2012) created the higher rates, plus a temporary sales tax, through 2018 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). It passed with 55.4% statewide and 60.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2012 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/15-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 55 (November 2016) extended the income tax rates through 2030 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). It passed with 63.3% statewide and 67.5% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2016 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/65-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by David Goldberg of the California Teachers Association, Katie Nilsson of the California School Nurses Organization and Jodi Hicks of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It “is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone”; without it, “millionaires and billionaires” get a tax cut.
Without it, schools face “billions in cuts,” and Medi-Cal “could be put at risk.”
The money goes “directly to local schools” and “the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it.”
It is “independently audited every year.”
Their rebuttal, signed by the presidents of the California Federation of Teachers, California Professional Firefighters and California School Employees Association, adds that it protects “firefighters and wildfire protection” by freeing state money (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Robert Gutierrez of the California Taxpayers Association, Robert Rivinius of the Family Business Association of California and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Voters were told the rates were temporary, “only for seven years,” then they were extended “for another 12 years.”
California has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes, and higher taxes raise the cost of living.
Spending “increased by $150 billion” since the rates began, and a “$100 billion budget surplus” became “a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years.”
“California’s population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.”
Their rebuttal to the argument in favor, signed by Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and two business group leaders, calls it “the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
CTA President David Goldberg told KCRA that without the measure services would be “cut across the board,” including “health care, resources for students and families” (New York Post, citing KCRA (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)).
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association President Jon Coupal said, “Proposition 3 is an extension of the existing tax rates, so its impact may not be as dramatic, but it still exists” (New York Post (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)). The association’s guide says the “temporary” rates “should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).

Proposition 3 : Make high-income tax rates permanent
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates on high earners that voters first approved in 2012 (Proposition 30) and extended in 2016 (Proposition 55). Those rates are now set to expire in 2031. They apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers (2025 levels, adjusted for inflation).
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 3
Who pays Top 2% of taxpayers: income over about $371,000 single or $742,000 joint (2025)
Revenue kept $5 billion to $15 billion a year starting in 2031 (Legislative Analyst)
Vote needed Simple majority
Money raised, Jan. 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $79.32 million (main committee). Against: $5,500
Largest donor California Teachers Association, $60.50 million (76.3%)
Outside spending Against: $53,500 by Reform California (shared with other props). For: about $155,000
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 58% yes, 41% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 54% yes, 37% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , The details , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 3 mean?
An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
What does a no vote on Proposition 3 mean?
An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
What would Proposition 3 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates the state would keep $5 billion to $15 billion a year in income tax revenue that would otherwise end in 2031. The amount would swing with the stock market. Roughly 40% would go to schools and community colleges, and the rest to other state programs, with part set aside in budget reserves.
What it means for the City of LA
The City of Los Angeles would not receive this money directly. The school share goes to school districts and community colleges, such as LAUSD and the Los Angeles Community College District, which are separate governments; the LAUSD board endorsed Proposition 3 in August 2026. The rest supports the state General Fund, which pays for state programs used in the City, including homelessness grants to local governments. City residents with incomes above the thresholds would keep paying the higher rates after 2031.
The details
Official title Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
This is not the Proposition 3 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the constitutional amendment on the right to marry, which passed with 62.6% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 3 passes
Top income tax rates 10.3%, 11.3% and 12.3% on income above the thresholds, through the 2030 tax year; they expire in 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The same rates, with no end date (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Who pays About the top 2% of taxpayers, who pay about half of all state income taxes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). 2025 thresholds: about $371,000 single, $742,000 joint, $505,000 head of household (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same, with thresholds still adjusted each year for inflation (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Revenue Recently about $10 billion a year, the Budget Center says (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) $5 billion to $15 billion a year kept after 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Where it goes Deposited in the Education Protection Account: 89% to K-12 schools, 11% to community colleges (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same. Because the money counts toward the state’s school funding guarantee, the Analyst says roughly 40% ends up as added school funding and the rest supports other programs and reserves (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Local control and audits School boards decide how to spend it in public meetings, may not use it for administrators’ pay, must post an annual accounting online, and must have it checked in their annual audit (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)) Unchanged (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6))
Medi-Cal formula from Prop 55 A formula that could send some revenue to Medi-Cal; the Budget Center says it has never done so (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The measure lets it expire (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/))
For the City of Los Angeles:
No money goes to the City directly. The school share is paid to school districts, county offices of education, charter schools and community college districts (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). In Los Angeles those are LAUSD and other districts, and the Los Angeles Community College District, which are separate from City government.
LAUSD’s position. The LAUSD Board of Education adopted a resolution in support of Proposition 3, introduced by board members Rivas and Schmerelson, on Aug. 25, 2026 (LAUSD Res-006-26/27 (https://lausd.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8145&GUID=AE05159C-03AD-47C2-B5B1-19227D526555)).
Through the state budget. The Budget Center says the revenue has freed General Fund money for other programs, and lists the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) grants to local governments among the programs created since 2012 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). The City budgets HHAP money (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf)). Neither the Analyst nor the Budget Center estimates the effect on any city.
Who in the City pays. City residents with taxable income above the thresholds would keep paying the higher rates. We did not find official data on how many City residents pay them.
We found no City Council position on Proposition 3 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 3 is a citizen initiative (No. 25-0016). It amends Section 36 of Article XIII of the State Constitution (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Nov. 4, 2025: The Attorney General issued the title and summary. The proponents are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Jan. 13, 2026: Proponents reported reaching 25% of the needed signatures (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
June 10, 2026: Counties’ random samples projected 1,151,120 valid signatures from 1,648,745 submitted, against 874,641 needed, so the measure became eligible. Los Angeles County received 454,802 signatures, 314,836 of them projected valid (SOS random sample count (http://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1993-randomsample-06-10-26.pdf)). The campaign paid Democracy Werks California 2024, LLC $17,435,148.50 for petition and related work (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The tax is a general income tax rate, not a local special tax, so the two-thirds rules for local special taxes and Proposition 43 do not apply to it (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Prop 43 title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 30 (November 2012) created the higher rates, plus a temporary sales tax, through 2018 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). It passed with 55.4% statewide and 60.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2012 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/15-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 55 (November 2016) extended the income tax rates through 2030 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). It passed with 63.3% statewide and 67.5% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2016 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/65-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by David Goldberg of the California Teachers Association, Katie Nilsson of the California School Nurses Organization and Jodi Hicks of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It “is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone”; without it, “millionaires and billionaires” get a tax cut.
Without it, schools face “billions in cuts,” and Medi-Cal “could be put at risk.”
The money goes “directly to local schools” and “the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it.”
It is “independently audited every year.”
Their rebuttal, signed by the presidents of the California Federation of Teachers, California Professional Firefighters and California School Employees Association, adds that it protects “firefighters and wildfire protection” by freeing state money (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Robert Gutierrez of the California Taxpayers Association, Robert Rivinius of the Family Business Association of California and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Voters were told the rates were temporary, “only for seven years,” then they were extended “for another 12 years.”
California has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes, and higher taxes raise the cost of living.
Spending “increased by $150 billion” since the rates began, and a “$100 billion budget surplus” became “a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years.”
“California’s population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.”
Their rebuttal to the argument in favor, signed by Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and two business group leaders, calls it “the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
CTA President David Goldberg told KCRA that without the measure services would be “cut across the board,” including “health care, resources for students and families” (New York Post, citing KCRA (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)).
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association President Jon Coupal said, “Proposition 3 is an extension of the existing tax rates, so its impact may not be as dramatic, but it still exists” (New York Post (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)). The association’s guide says the “temporary” rates “should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What the records show
Not a new tax; does not raise anyone’s taxes Yes campaign The rates are in effect now. Prop 3 removes the 2031 end date (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). Taxpayers above the thresholds would pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more after 2031 than if the rates expired (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Up to $15 billion a year; largest permanent income tax increase No campaign The Analyst’s range is $5 billion to $15 billion a year (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). We did not find an official ranking of tax increases.
The money goes directly to schools and the Legislature cannot touch it Yes campaign The Education Protection Account sends the money to schools and colleges and bars its use for state costs (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). The Analyst says that, because it counts toward the school funding guarantee, about 40% becomes added school funding and the rest supports other state programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Audited every year, with criminal penalties for misuse Yes campaign Local annual audits must check the money, the Controller shall audit the account, and the Attorney General or district attorneys may seek civil or criminal penalties for misuse (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=7)).
Temporary for seven years, then extended 12 more No campaign Prop 30’s income tax rates ran through 2018; Prop 55 extended them through 2030 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Only the top 2% pay Yes campaign The Analyst says the top 2% of taxpayers pay these rates (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
We did not check the “$100 billion surplus to $30 billion deficit,” “$150 billion” spending growth or population figures against official budget records.

Supporters
On the ballot label: California Teachers Association, California School Nurses Organization, California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/)).
Named in the argument in favor: California Federation of Teachers, California Nurses Association, California School Employees Association, Community College League of California and Nurse Alliance of SEIU California (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). California Professional Firefighters signed the rebuttal (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
League of Women Voters of California (LWVC recommendations (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/)).
California State PTA, which voted to support in February 2026 (CAPTA (https://capta.org/advocacy/state-ballot-measures/)).

Top income tax rates 10.3%, 11.3% and 12.3% on income above the thresholds, through the 2030 tax year; they expire in 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The same rates, with no end date (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Who pays About the top 2% of taxpayers, who pay about half of all state income taxes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). 2025 thresholds: about $371,000 single, $742,000 joint, $505,000 head of household (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same, with thresholds still adjusted each year for inflation (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Revenue Recently about $10 billion a year, the Budget Center says (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) $5 billion to $15 billion a year kept after 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Where it goes Deposited in the Education Protection Account: 89% to K-12 schools, 11% to community colleges (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same. Because the money counts toward the state’s school funding guarantee, the Analyst says roughly 40% ends up as added school funding and the rest supports other programs and reserves (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Local control and audits School boards decide how to spend it in public meetings, may not use it for administrators’ pay, must post an annual accounting online, and must have it checked in their annual audit (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)) Unchanged (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6))
Medi-Cal formula from Prop 55 A formula that could send some revenue to Medi-Cal; the Budget Center says it has never done so (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The measure lets it expire (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/))
For the City of Los Angeles:
No money goes to the City directly. The school share is paid to school districts, county offices of education, charter schools and community college districts (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). In Los Angeles those are LAUSD and other districts, and the Los Angeles Community College District, which are separate from City government.
LAUSD’s position. The LAUSD Board of Education adopted a resolution in support of Proposition 3, introduced by board members Rivas and Schmerelson, on Aug. 25, 2026 (LAUSD Res-006-26/27 (https://lausd.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8145&GUID=AE05159C-03AD-47C2-B5B1-19227D526555)).
Through the state budget. The Budget Center says the revenue has freed General Fund money for other programs, and lists the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) grants to local governments among the programs created since 2012 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). The City budgets HHAP money (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf)). Neither the Analyst nor the Budget Center estimates the effect on any city.
Who in the City pays. City residents with taxable income above the thresholds would keep paying the higher rates. We did not find official data on how many City residents pay them.
We found no City Council position on Proposition 3 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 3 is a citizen initiative (No. 25-0016). It amends Section 36 of Article XIII of the State Constitution (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Nov. 4, 2025: The Attorney General issued the title and summary. The proponents are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Jan. 13, 2026: Proponents reported reaching 25% of the needed signatures (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
June 10, 2026: Counties’ random samples projected 1,151,120 valid signatures from 1,648,745 submitted, against 874,641 needed, so the measure became eligible. Los Angeles County received 454,802 signatures, 314,836 of them projected valid (SOS random sample count (http://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1993-randomsample-06-10-26.pdf)). The campaign paid Democracy Werks California 2024, LLC $17,435,148.50 for petition and related work (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The tax is a general income tax rate, not a local special tax, so the two-thirds rules for local special taxes and Proposition 43 do not apply to it (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Prop 43 title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 30 (November 2012) created the higher rates, plus a temporary sales tax, through 2018 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). It passed with 55.4% statewide and 60.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2012 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/15-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 55 (November 2016) extended the income tax rates through 2030 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). It passed with 63.3% statewide and 67.5% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2016 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/65-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by David Goldberg of the California Teachers Association, Katie Nilsson of the California School Nurses Organization and Jodi Hicks of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It “is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone”; without it, “millionaires and billionaires” get a tax cut.
Without it, schools face “billions in cuts,” and Medi-Cal “could be put at risk.”
The money goes “directly to local schools” and “the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it.”
It is “independently audited every year.”
Their rebuttal, signed by the presidents of the California Federation of Teachers, California Professional Firefighters and California School Employees Association, adds that it protects “firefighters and wildfire protection” by freeing state money (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Robert Gutierrez of the California Taxpayers Association, Robert Rivinius of the Family Business Association of California and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Voters were told the rates were temporary, “only for seven years,” then they were extended “for another 12 years.”
California has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes, and higher taxes raise the cost of living.
Spending “increased by $150 billion” since the rates began, and a “$100 billion budget surplus” became “a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years.”
“California’s population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.”
Their rebuttal to the argument in favor, signed by Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and two business group leaders, calls it “the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
CTA President David Goldberg told KCRA that without the measure services would be “cut across the board,” including “health care, resources for students and families” (New York Post, citing KCRA (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)).
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association President Jon Coupal said, “Proposition 3 is an extension of the existing tax rates, so its impact may not be as dramatic, but it still exists” (New York Post (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)). The association’s guide says the “temporary” rates “should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What the records show
Not a new tax; does not raise anyone’s taxes Yes campaign The rates are in effect now. Prop 3 removes the 2031 end date (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). Taxpayers above the thresholds would pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more after 2031 than if the rates expired (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Up to $15 billion a year; largest permanent income tax increase No campaign The Analyst’s range is $5 billion to $15 billion a year (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). We did not find an official ranking of tax increases.
The money goes directly to schools and the Legislature cannot touch it Yes campaign The Education Protection Account sends the money to schools and colleges and bars its use for state costs (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). The Analyst says that, because it counts toward the school funding guarantee, about 40% becomes added school funding and the rest supports other state programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Audited every year, with criminal penalties for misuse Yes campaign Local annual audits must check the money, the Controller shall audit the account, and the Attorney General or district attorneys may seek civil or criminal penalties for misuse (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=7)).
Temporary for seven years, then extended 12 more No campaign Prop 30’s income tax rates ran through 2018; Prop 55 extended them through 2030 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Only the top 2% pay Yes campaign The Analyst says the top 2% of taxpayers pay these rates (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
We did not check the “$100 billion surplus to $30 billion deficit,” “$150 billion” spending growth or population figures against official budget records.
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
On the ballot label: California Teachers Association, California School Nurses Organization, California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/)).
Named in the argument in favor: California Federation of Teachers, California Nurses Association, California School Employees Association, Community College League of California and Nurse Alliance of SEIU California (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)). California Professional Firefighters signed the rebuttal (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
League of Women Voters of California (LWVC recommendations (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/)).
California State PTA, which voted to support in February 2026 (CAPTA (https://capta.org/advocacy/state-ballot-measures/)).
LAUSD Board of Education (LAUSD Res-006-26/27 (https://lausd.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8145&GUID=AE05159C-03AD-47C2-B5B1-19227D526555)).
Xavier Becerra, candidate for governor, supports Proposition 3 and opposes Proposition 40, the New York Post reported (New York Post (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)).
The Los Angeles County Federation of Labor reported spending for it (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
On the ballot label: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/)).

Proposition 3 : Make high-income tax rates permanent
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates on high earners that voters first approved in 2012 (Proposition 30) and extended in 2016 (Proposition 55). Those rates are now set to expire in 2031. They apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers (2025 levels, adjusted for inflation).
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 3
Who pays Top 2% of taxpayers: income over about $371,000 single or $742,000 joint (2025)
Revenue kept $5 billion to $15 billion a year starting in 2031 (Legislative Analyst)
Vote needed Simple majority
Money raised, Jan. 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $79.32 million (main committee). Against: $5,500
Largest donor California Teachers Association, $60.50 million (76.3%)
Outside spending Against: $53,500 by Reform California (shared with other props). For: about $155,000
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 58% yes, 41% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 54% yes, 37% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , The details , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 3 mean?
An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
What does a no vote on Proposition 3 mean?
An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
What would Proposition 3 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates the state would keep $5 billion to $15 billion a year in income tax revenue that would otherwise end in 2031. The amount would swing with the stock market. Roughly 40% would go to schools and community colleges, and the rest to other state programs, with part set aside in budget reserves.
What it means for the City of LA
The City of Los Angeles would not receive this money directly. The school share goes to school districts and community colleges, such as LAUSD and the Los Angeles Community College District, which are separate governments; the LAUSD board endorsed Proposition 3 in August 2026. The rest supports the state General Fund, which pays for state programs used in the City, including homelessness grants to local governments. City residents with incomes above the thresholds would keep paying the higher rates after 2031.
The details
Official title Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Initiative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
This is not the Proposition 3 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the constitutional amendment on the right to marry, which passed with 62.6% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 3 passes
Top income tax rates 10.3%, 11.3% and 12.3% on income above the thresholds, through the 2030 tax year; they expire in 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The same rates, with no end date (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Who pays About the top 2% of taxpayers, who pay about half of all state income taxes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). 2025 thresholds: about $371,000 single, $742,000 joint, $505,000 head of household (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same, with thresholds still adjusted each year for inflation (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm))
Revenue Recently about $10 billion a year, the Budget Center says (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) $5 billion to $15 billion a year kept after 2031 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Where it goes Deposited in the Education Protection Account: 89% to K-12 schools, 11% to community colleges (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm)) Same. Because the money counts toward the state’s school funding guarantee, the Analyst says roughly 40% ends up as added school funding and the rest supports other programs and reserves (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm))
Local control and audits School boards decide how to spend it in public meetings, may not use it for administrators’ pay, must post an annual accounting online, and must have it checked in their annual audit (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)) Unchanged (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6))
Medi-Cal formula from Prop 55 A formula that could send some revenue to Medi-Cal; the Budget Center says it has never done so (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)) The measure lets it expire (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/))
For the City of Los Angeles:
No money goes to the City directly. The school share is paid to school districts, county offices of education, charter schools and community college districts (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). In Los Angeles those are LAUSD and other districts, and the Los Angeles Community College District, which are separate from City government.
LAUSD’s position. The LAUSD Board of Education adopted a resolution in support of Proposition 3, introduced by board members Rivas and Schmerelson, on Aug. 25, 2026 (LAUSD Res-006-26/27 (https://lausd.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8145&GUID=AE05159C-03AD-47C2-B5B1-19227D526555)).
Through the state budget. The Budget Center says the revenue has freed General Fund money for other programs, and lists the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) grants to local governments among the programs created since 2012 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). The City budgets HHAP money (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf)). Neither the Analyst nor the Budget Center estimates the effect on any city.
Who in the City pays. City residents with taxable income above the thresholds would keep paying the higher rates. We did not find official data on how many City residents pay them.
We found no City Council position on Proposition 3 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 3 is a citizen initiative (No. 25-0016). It amends Section 36 of Article XIII of the State Constitution (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3)).
Nov. 4, 2025: The Attorney General issued the title and summary. The proponents are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures); argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Jan. 13, 2026: Proponents reported reaching 25% of the needed signatures (SOS eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
June 10, 2026: Counties’ random samples projected 1,151,120 valid signatures from 1,648,745 submitted, against 874,641 needed, so the measure became eligible. Los Angeles County received 454,802 signatures, 314,836 of them projected valid (SOS random sample count (http://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/1993-randomsample-06-10-26.pdf)). The campaign paid Democracy Werks California 2024, LLC $17,435,148.50 for petition and related work (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The tax is a general income tax rate, not a local special tax, so the two-thirds rules for local special taxes and Proposition 43 do not apply to it (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm); Prop 43 title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 30 (November 2012) created the higher rates, plus a temporary sales tax, through 2018 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/)). It passed with 55.4% statewide and 60.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2012 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/15-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 55 (November 2016) extended the income tax rates through 2030 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). It passed with 63.3% statewide and 67.5% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2016 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/65-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by David Goldberg of the California Teachers Association, Katie Nilsson of the California School Nurses Organization and Jodi Hicks of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It “is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone”; without it, “millionaires and billionaires” get a tax cut.
Without it, schools face “billions in cuts,” and Medi-Cal “could be put at risk.”
The money goes “directly to local schools” and “the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it.”
It is “independently audited every year.”
Their rebuttal, signed by the presidents of the California Federation of Teachers, California Professional Firefighters and California School Employees Association, adds that it protects “firefighters and wildfire protection” by freeing state money (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Robert Gutierrez of the California Taxpayers Association, Robert Rivinius of the Family Business Association of California and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Voters were told the rates were temporary, “only for seven years,” then they were extended “for another 12 years.”
California has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes, and higher taxes raise the cost of living.
Spending “increased by $150 billion” since the rates began, and a “$100 billion budget surplus” became “a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years.”
“California’s population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.”
Their rebuttal to the argument in favor, signed by Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and two business group leaders, calls it “the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
CTA President David Goldberg told KCRA that without the measure services would be “cut across the board,” including “health care, resources for students and families” (New York Post, citing KCRA (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)).
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association President Jon Coupal said, “Proposition 3 is an extension of the existing tax rates, so its impact may not be as dramatic, but it still exists” (New York Post (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/temporary-california-tax-is-set-to-expire-but-democrats-want-to-make-it-permanent/ar-AA2bGHtV)). The association’s guide says the “temporary” rates “should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What the records show
Not a new tax; does not raise anyone’s taxes Yes campaign The rates are in effect now. Prop 3 removes the 2031 end date (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). Taxpayers above the thresholds would pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more after 2031 than if the rates expired (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Up to $15 billion a year; largest permanent income tax increase No campaign The Analyst’s range is $5 billion to $15 billion a year (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)). We did not find an official ranking of tax increases.
The money goes directly to schools and the Legislature cannot touch it Yes campaign The Education Protection Account sends the money to schools and colleges and bars its use for state costs (text, Sec. 4 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). The Analyst says that, because it counts toward the school funding guarantee, about 40% becomes added school funding and the rest supports other state programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Audited every year, with criminal penalties for misuse Yes campaign Local annual audits must check the money, the Controller shall audit the account, and the Attorney General or district attorneys may seek civil or criminal penalties for misuse (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=7)).
Temporary for seven years, then extended 12 more No campaign Prop 30’s income tax rates ran through 2018; Prop 55 extended them through 2030 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
Only the top 2% pay Yes campaign The Analyst says the top 2% of taxpayers pay these rates (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/analysis.htm)).
We did not check the “$100 billion surplus to $30 billion deficit,” “$150 billion” spending growth or population figures against official budget records.

PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal Impact : Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters : California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents : California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
CON
Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

### Additional Titles

Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering.

The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
